analysis.one_liner: Gives the Agriculture Secretary power to order recalls of contaminated meat and poultry and fine violators.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Agriculture Committee: introduced with 15 Democratic senators behind it, it died without a hearing, a vote, or a House companion.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the law at the time, the Department of Agriculture could inspect meat and poultry plants but had no power to force a company to recall contaminated product — it could only ask. This bill would have required companies to notify the Secretary of Agriculture when they had reason to believe their meat or poultry was adulterated, let the Secretary order distribution stopped and recall tainted product, pull federal inspectors from repeat-offender plants, and impose civil fines of up to $100,000 per violation, with each day of violation counting separately. It applied the same rules to meat and to poultry.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers of meat and poultry — essentially everyone. The bill aimed to get contaminated products off shelves faster and to warn people who may have already bought them, rather than relying on companies to recall voluntarily. Taxpayers also benefit indirectly from fewer foodborne illness outbreaks to respond to.

how_it_helps.text: Requires any business in the meat and poultry supply chain to immediately notify the Secretary of Agriculture when it has reason to believe a product is adulterated or misbranded [S3].
Lets the Secretary order companies to stop distributing tainted product and recall it, first voluntarily and then by mandatory order if they refuse or delay [S3].
Requires consumer notice to people who may have bought or eaten the affected product [S3].
Allows the Secretary to suspend or withdraw inspection from plants that willfully or repeatedly violate the law, which would halt their legal ability to ship product [S3].
Adds civil penalties of up to $100,000 per violation, with each day of a continuing violation counted as a separate offense, and lets the Attorney General sue to collect unpaid fines [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Meat and poultry processors and distributors, who would face recall orders, possible loss of inspection (shutting down shipments), and fines. Some costs would likely be passed to consumers in meat prices, though the bill let the Secretary scale penalties to the size and type of business.

drawbacks.text: Recall orders and inspection withdrawals could hit a plant's entire operation on the Secretary's judgment that there is a 'reasonable probability' of a public health threat; companies got an informal hearing only within two days after the order took effect, and review of inspection-withdrawal orders happens in the courts of appeals rather than district court, limiting their chance to contest first [S3].

Fines of up to $100,000 per violation, per day, could stack heavily on small processors, although the bill required the Secretary to weigh the gravity of the violation, culpability, business size, and prior history [S3].
Notification duties fall on businesses throughout the supply chain, adding compliance paperwork and legal risk for distributors and retailers who did not produce the tainted product [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is speed of getting contaminated food off shelves versus the business cost of government-ordered recalls. The bill built in checks — a hearing within two days, judicial review, penalties scaled to firm size — but the mandatory recall and inspector-withdrawal powers were a real expansion of government control over plants. For consumers, the benefit is avoiding foodborne illness from products that under then-current law the government could only ask companies to pull voluntarily.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Agriculture Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the 106th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Harkin introduced the bill on January 19, 1999, joined by 13 other Democratic senators as original sponsors [S1].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry on the day of introduction [S5].
No further action — no hearing, no committee report, no floor vote — appears in the bill's action history for the rest of the Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Meat and poultry processors are better off: they kept the status quo in which the government could not force a recall of contaminated product, and companies facing mandatory notification duties, recall orders, and per-day civil fines avoided all of them. Consumers gained nothing from the bill's failure.

for.name: Sen. Tom Harkin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the SAFER Meat and Poultry Act and delivered introductory remarks on it.

for.name: 15 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including the Senate Democratic leader, Tom Daschle, as an original sponsor.

against.name: Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican in the 106th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no action on it — no hearing or markup — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Meat and poultry processing industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed giving the Agriculture Secretary mandatory recall authority over meat and poultry products, a position widely reported during the debate over USDA recall powers in the 1990s.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 sponsors and cosponsors — Sen. Harkin plus 15 cosponsors — were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced past the Republican-chaired Agriculture Committee.

industries.note: The bill would have forced processors to flag suspected contamination, halted distribution of tainted product on government order, and exposed them to per-day fines and loss of inspection. Its failure left them without mandatory recall or notification duties. Consumers' interest in fast recalls of contaminated meat runs directly against processors' interest in controlling their own recalls.

industries.industry: Meat and poultry distributors, wholesalers, and retailers
industries.note: Notified businesses would have been required to immediately stop distributing any product named in an order, creating compliance costs and inventory losses. They also benefit from consumer confidence when tainted product is pulled quickly.
